source.title: Alternating Gradient Flows: A Theory of Feature Learning in Two-layer Neural Networks
source.authors: Daniel Kunin; Giovanni Luca Marchetti; Feng Chen; Dhruva Karkada; James B. Simon; M. R. DeWeese; Surya Ganguli; N. Miolane

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a theoretical and numerical account of Fourier-feature emergence during modular-addition training, using Alternating Gradient Flows rather than the original grokking measurements. It bears on V2, but does not measure delayed test generalization.
record.gate_note: The modular-addition analysis reports Fourier-feature order and AGF predictions of feature-acquisition timing. It does not report train/test accuracy, overfitting followed by delayed generalization, or a training-set-size sweep. The CIFAR-10 experiment reports training-loss dynamics, not generalization delay, so it is not a V3 result. Results cited from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper trains a two-layer quadratic network on the entire modular-addition dataset of p² pairs, with no held-out set. It therefore cannot show memorization, delayed test generalization, or memorizing components being removed. Its result is that training loss falls stepwise, saddle to saddle, as Fourier features are acquired in decreasing order of coefficient magnitude. That is a feature-learning result on training dynamics, a related but different construct from grokking. It cites Power et al. and Nanda et al. as background only.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors present AGF as a framework that approximates gradient flow at small initialization and predicts the order, timing and size of loss drops. It provably matches GF for diagonal linear networks and recovers prior linear-network and linear-transformer results. For quadratic networks on modular addition, it shows Fourier features learned in decreasing order of coefficient magnitude. They note that general AGF–GF correspondence is open and may fail on natural data and deeper architectures.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes a two-layer quadratic network using AGF and gradient-flow dynamics on the entire modular-addition dataset. It does not use the original grokking train/test-accuracy protocol or measure a delayed generalization transition.
record.method_sensitivity: The modular-addition theoretical result assumes centered inputs and distinct magnitudes for non-conjugate Fourier coefficients; its cost-minimization analysis assumes activated neurons remain aligned to a harmonic. The separate CIFAR-10 loss-curve experiment reports that the stepwise appearance changes with hidden width.

fits_no_version.finding: On full-dataset modular addition, a small-initialization quadratic network acquires Fourier features one frequency group at a time, in decreasing order of |x̂[ξ]|. Each acquisition comes with a training-loss drop after a plateau. AGF predicts the order, levels and approximate timing, and closely tracks GD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fourier features for modular arithmetic emerge through saddle-to-saddle training dynamics, ordered by input-encoding coefficient magnitude, independent of any generalization gap.

fits_no_version.finding: On a CIFAR-10 subset with a two-layer ReLU network, training-loss curves are stepwise at small width but become smooth slides as width grows, and AGF's correspondence with GD weakens (Fig. 7). This is training loss only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stepwise feature-acquisition loss curves at small initialization depend on width and smooth out in wider networks on natural data.

record.problems: The paper does not measure the grokking train/test-accuracy pattern. Its authors state that general AGF-to-gradient-flow correspondence remains open. The modular-addition cost-minimization analysis restricts attention to aligned neurons, and the numerical comparison is presented in a figure without numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows omitted. The CIFAR-10 width experiment is not included because it reports training-loss shape rather than a result measuring delayed generalization.

untested.parts: Formation of the generalizing circuit relative to memorization, removal of memorizing components, and progress measures anticipating a held-out accuracy jump. None is possible because training uses the full dataset.
Delayed test-accuracy jump and its dependence on training-set size. There is no train/test split.

record.verdict_notes: Not a grokking test: there is no held-out set, and the 'jumps' are training-loss drops, not test-accuracy jumps. The record's 'tests/T2' and its V2 labels should be dropped. The Fig. 6 experiment uses p=20 and a three-cosine template, not one-hot encoding.

versions.untested_parts: No train/test accuracy, overfitting point, delayed test-accuracy rise, or training-set-size comparison is reported.

The paper analyzes Fourier-feature emergence and AGF jump-time predictions, but does not track memorizing components being removed, nor test whether empirical continuous progress measures anticipate a held-out-accuracy jump.

The CIFAR-10 experiment varies hidden width and reports training loss, but does not test delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data or switching such delays through initialization scale or weight norm.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning experiment is reported.
The paper does not test weight decay or another low-norm bias as an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The paper does not compare algorithms learned across runs or test convergence to the same identifiable algorithm.
The paper does not test adaptive-optimizer instability, floating-point softmax limits, or other proposed numerical artifacts of grokking.

conditions.value: entire modular-addition dataset of p² pairs
centered vector x; non-conjugate Fourier coefficients have distinct magnitudes

rows.value: AGF predicts sequential acquisition of frequencies in decreasing order of |x̂[ξ]|.
rows.locator: Section 5, AGF in action: greedy Fourier decomposition; Equation (9)
rows.note: This is a theoretical characterization of feature acquisition, not a measurement of held-out accuracy or a grokking delay.
rows.check: This is a theoretical AGF prediction (Eq. 9) of the order of Fourier features on the full dataset. It has no train/test split and no generalization measure, so it cannot bear on V2's generalizing-vs-memorizing account or on progress measures anticipating a test-accuracy jump.

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic network trained by gradient descent
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition and track the output power spectrum

conditions.value: template has x̂[1] = 10, x̂[3] = 5, and x̂[5] = 2.5

rows.note: The text describes sequential learning of the template's Fourier components, with dominant frequencies learned first. The plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: This is the gradient-descent power spectrum on the full p=20 dataset (Fig. 6a), showing stepwise acquisition of dominant frequencies. No held-out accuracy is measured, so it does not bear on V2. Note that p=20 is even, although the theory assumes odd p.
